# Three ways to index a vector

A vector index speeds up nearest-neighbor search by examining only a small part of the table, at the
cost of sometimes missing a true neighbor. Postgres can index a `vector` column in three ways. HNSW
comes with pgvector, DiskANN with Timescale's pgvectorscale, and PRISM with the newer
pg_vectorsearch. The first two are graphs that a query walks, and the third is a set of partitions
that a query scans.

## Index designs

**HNSW** (pgvector) is a layered proximity graph. A query enters at the sparse top layer and moves
down towards the dense bottom one, keeping `ef_search` candidates as it goes. The graph needs no
training pass, so inserts stay cheap, and two settings, `m` (the links per node) and
`ef_construction`, trade build time for recall.

**DiskANN** (pgvectorscale 0.9.1) is a single flat graph, designed to stay fast when the index does
not fit in memory. It stores compressed vectors in the index (statistical binary quantization) and
reads the full vectors only to rescore the best candidates.

**PRISM** (pg_vectorsearch 0.1.0, alpha, Postgres 18 only) partitions the table instead of building a
graph. k-means splits the rows into `nlist` partitions, in the style of an IVF index, and each vector
is stored as a RaBitQ code with an error bound. A query scans the `prism.nprobe` nearest partitions
and reads full vectors only for candidates that the error bound cannot settle. PRISM indexes
pgvector's column in place, and creating and tuning it takes three statements:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON demo_docs USING prism (embedding vec32_cosine_ops);  -- build after loading
SET prism.nprobe = 40;                                               -- 0 = auto
SELECT * FROM prism_index_settings('demo_docs_embedding_idx');       -- what it chose, and why
```

## Build time and recall

The lab built all three indexes on 20,000 random 64-dimensional unit vectors on Postgres 18, in one
run on a laptop, and measured recall@10 (the share of the exact top 10 that the index returns)
against an exact scan:

| index | build | size | best recall@10 | ms per query at best |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HNSW (m 16, ef_construction 64) | 2.7 s | 11.4 MB | 0.99 (ef_search 400) | 3.3 |
| DiskANN (defaults) | 20.3 s | 9.1 MB | 0.76 (search list 400, rescore 400) | 8.3 |
| PRISM (auto nlist 144) | 0.3 s | 1.8 MB | 0.98 (nprobe 160, every list) | 3.0 |

PRISM built about nine times faster than HNSW and took about a sixth of its size, and its recall
came close to HNSW's once every partition was probed. With the automatic `nprobe` (10 here) it
reached only about 0.40, rising to 0.81 at 40 and 0.93 at 80.

::: {.callout-important}
## The test data

Random vectors are the hardest case for both quantization and partitioning. Their coordinates are
independent, so binary codes have nothing to capture and k-means has no clusters to follow, which is
why DiskANN stalls at 0.76 and PRISM needs every partition. Real embeddings cluster strongly, so both
indexes should do better on them, although the lab did not measure that. PRISM's automatic `nprobe`
aims at a recall of about 0.95.
:::

## Choosing an index

HNSW is the usual choice, since it needs no training, is mature, and gives good recall at any size
that fits in memory. DiskANN suits an index too large for RAM, if its slower build is acceptable.
PRISM suits frequent rebuilds or many tables, where build time and size matter, on Postgres 18 and
with the caveat that an alpha release may need `DROP EXTENSION` and a rebuild between versions. In
SQLAlchemy all three are an `Index(...)` with `postgresql_using` and `postgresql_ops`, and the
queries stay the same.
